'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities **Ame no Mikumari no Kami** (天水分神) and **Kuni no Mikumari no Kami** (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

{{draft}}[[fr:Mikumari]] {{Infobox deity|image=File:Udamikumari Shr Kami.jpg|script=水分神|name=Mikumari-no-Kami|script_name=Japanese|mother={{ill|Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime}}|father={{ill|Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko}}|temples={{ill|Kono Shrine|en|Kono Shrine|fr|Kono-jinja|ja|籠神社|simple|user:immanuelle/Kono Shrine}} {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} {{ill|Katsuragi Mikumari Shrine|ja|葛木水分神社}} {{ill|Tsuge Mikumari Shrine|ja|都祁水分神社}} {{ill|Take Mikumari Shrine|ja|建水分神社}}}} {{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} '''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous **mikumari** shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities **Ame no Mikumari no Kami** (天水分神) and **Kuni no Mikumari no Kami** (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

The most famous **mikumari** shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities **Ame no Mikumari no Kami** (天水分神) and **Kuni no Mikumari no Kami** (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]
==Overview== [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ Unlinked]] [[Category:Mikumari]][[category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Image:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|thumb|right|250px|Kami-umi mythology (神産み) showing the gods born of Izanagi and Izanami. [[media:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|View as SVG (supported browsers only)]]]]
'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]
==Overview== [[Category:Mikumari]][[category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Image:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|thumb|right|250px|Kami-umi mythology (神産み) showing the gods born of Izanagi and Izanami. [[media:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|View as SVG (supported browsers only)]]]]
'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]
==Overview== [[Category:Mikumari]][[category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Image:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|thumb|right|250px|Kami-umi mythology (神産み) showing the gods born of Izanagi and Izanami. [[media:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|View as SVG (supported browsers only)]]]]
'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]
==Overview== [[Category:Mikumari]][[category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Image:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|thumb|right|250px|Kami-umi mythology (神産み) showing the gods born of Izanagi and Izanami. [[media:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|View as SVG (supported browsers only)]]]]
'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]
==Overview== [[Category:Mikumari]][[category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Image:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|thumb|right|250px|Kami-umi mythology (神産み) showing the gods born of Izanagi and Izanami. [[media:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|View as SVG (supported browsers only)]]]]
'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602qq5915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=97qq|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602qq5915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=97qq|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602qq5915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=97qq|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602qq5915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=97qq|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:36, 18 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox deity|image=File:Udamikumari Shr Kami.jpg|script=水分神|name=Mikumari-no-Kami|script_name=Japanese|mother={{ill|Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime}}|father={{ill|Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko}}|temples={{ill|Kono Shrine|en|Kono Shrine|fr|Kono-jinja|ja|籠神社|simple|user:immanuelle/Kono Shrine}} {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} {{ill|Katsuragi Mikumari Shrine|ja|葛木水分神社}} {{ill|Tsuge Mikumari Shrine|ja|都祁水分神社}} {{ill|Take Mikumari Shrine|ja|建水分神社|1=Take Mikumari Shrine}}}} {{complex}}
'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602qq5915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=97qq|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]
==Overview== [[Category:Mikumari]][[Category:Unsorted]][[Category:Completion tier 2]][[Category:tier 2]] [[Category: Completion categories]]
[[Category:qq deprecated open]]<!--Mikumari--> [[Image:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|thumb|right|250px|Kami-umi mythology (神産み) showing the gods born of Izanagi and Izanami. [[media:Descendants of Izanagi and Izanami.svg|View as SVG (supported browsers only)]]]]
'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari no Kami''' (水分神) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} deity associated with the control and distribution of {{ill|water|ja|水}}. The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}}, during the {{ill|Kami-umi|ja|神産み}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|lt=rice field deities|ja|田の神}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|children|ja|子供}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602qq5915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=97qq|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[pregnancy]] and [[childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[water]] [[distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|4=fr|6=ja|7=水神}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> [[en:draft:Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami]]
