'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[:en:Pregnancy|Pregnancy]] and [[:en:Childbirth|Childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[:en:Water|Water]] [[:en:Distribution|Distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to [[:en:Suijin|Suijin]] who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In [[:en:Japanese mythology|Japanese mythology]], during the [[:en:Kamiumi|Kami-umi]] (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=rainmaking rites|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with [[:en:Ta-no-Kami|rice field deities]] or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of [[:en:Child|children]] and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[:en:Pregnancy|Pregnancy]] and [[:en:Childbirth|Childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[:en:Water|Water]] [[:en:Distribution|Distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to [[:en:Suijin|Suijin]] who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In [[:en:Japanese mythology|Japanese mythology]], during the [[:en:Kamiumi|Kami-umi]] (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=rainmaking rites|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with [[:en:Ta-no-Kami|rice field deities]] or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of [[:en:Child|children]] and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with [[:en:Pregnancy|Pregnancy]] and [[:en:Childbirth|Childbirth]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means [[:en:Water|Water]] [[:en:Distribution|Distribution]].<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to [[:en:Suijin|Suijin]] who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In [[:en:Japanese mythology|Japanese mythology]], during the [[:en:Kamiumi|Kami-umi]] (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=rainmaking rites|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with [[:en:Ta-no-Kami|rice field deities]] or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of [[:en:Child|children]] and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with {{ill|Pregnancy|en|Pregnancy|WD=Q11995|lt=Pregnancy}} and {{ill|Childbirth|en|Childbirth|WD=Q34581|lt=Childbirth}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means {{ill|Water|en|Water|WD=Q283|lt=Water}} {{ill|Distribution|en|Distribution|WD=Q225802|lt=Distribution}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|Suijin|WD=Q3137449|lt=Suijin}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|en|Japanese mythology|WD=Q814158|lt=Japanese mythology}}, during the {{ill|Kamiumi|en|Kamiumi|WD=Q3545159|lt=Kami-umi}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=rainmaking rites|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|en|Ta-no-Kami|WD=Q7683716|lt=rice field deities}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|Child|en|Child|WD=Q7569|lt=children}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with {{ill|Pregnancy|en|Pregnancy|WD=Q11995|lt=Pregnancy}} and {{ill|Childbirth|en|Childbirth|WD=Q34581|lt=Childbirth}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>
The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means {{ill|Water|en|Water|WD=Q283|lt=Water}} {{ill|Distribution|en|Distribution|WD=Q225802|lt=Distribution}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|Suijin|WD=Q3137449|lt=Suijin}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>
In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />
Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|en|Japanese mythology|WD=Q814158|lt=Japanese mythology}}, during the {{ill|Kamiumi|en|Kamiumi|WD=Q3545159|lt=Kami-umi}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.
As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=rainmaking rites|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|en|Ta-no-Kami|WD=Q7683716|lt=rice field deities}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|Child|en|Child|WD=Q7569|lt=children}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with {{ill|Pregnancy|en|Pregnancy|WD=Q11995|lt=Pregnancy}} and {{ill|Childbirth|en|Childbirth|WD=Q34581|lt=Childbirth}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means {{ill|Water|en|Water|WD=Q283|lt=Water}} {{ill|Distribution|en|Distribution|WD=Q225802|lt=Distribution}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|Suijin|WD=Q3137449|lt=Suijin}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In {{ill|Japanese mythology|en|Japanese mythology|WD=Q814158|lt=Japanese mythology}}, during the {{ill|Kamiumi|en|Kamiumi|WD=Q3545159|lt=Kami-umi}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=rainmaking rites|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|en|Ta-no-Kami|WD=Q7683716|lt=rice field deities}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|Child|en|Child|WD=Q7569|lt=children}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with {{ill|Pregnancy|en|Pregnancy|WD=Q11995|lt=Pregnancy}} and {{ill|Childbirth|en|Childbirth|WD=Q34581|lt=Childbirth}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means {{ill|Water|en|Water|WD=Q283|lt=Water}} {{ill|Distribution|en|Distribution|WD=Q225802|lt=Distribution}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|Suijin|WD=Q3137449|lt=Suijin}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In {{ill|Japanese mythology|en|Japanese mythology|WD=Q814158|lt=Japanese mythology}}, during the {{ill|Kamiumi|en|Kamiumi|WD=Q3545159|lt=Kami-umi}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=rainmaking rites|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|en|Ta-no-Kami|WD=Q7683716|lt=rice field deities}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|Child|en|Child|WD=Q7569|lt=children}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with {{ill|Pregnancy|en|Pregnancy|WD=Q11995|lt=Pregnancy}} and {{ill|Childbirth|en|Childbirth|WD=Q34581|lt=Childbirth}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means {{ill|Water|en|Water|WD=Q283|lt=Water}} {{ill|Distribution|en|Distribution|WD=Q225802|lt=Distribution}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|Suijin|WD=Q3137449|lt=Suijin}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> 

==Overview==

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In {{ill|Japanese mythology|en|Japanese mythology|WD=Q814158|lt=Japanese mythology}}, during the {{ill|Kamiumi|en|Kamiumi|WD=Q3545159|lt=Kami-umi}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=rainmaking rites|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|en|Ta-no-Kami|WD=Q7683716|lt=rice field deities}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|Child|en|Child|WD=Q7569|lt=children}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with {{ill|Pregnancy|en|Pregnancy|WD=Q11995|lt=Pregnancy}} and {{ill|Childbirth|en|Childbirth|WD=Q34581|lt=Childbirth}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means {{ill|Water|en|Water|WD=Q283|lt=Water}} {{ill|Distribution|en|Distribution|WD=Q225802|lt=Distribution}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|Suijin|WD=Q3137449|lt=Suijin}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In {{ill|Japanese mythology|en|Japanese mythology|WD=Q814158|lt=Japanese mythology}}, during the {{ill|Kamiumi|en|Kamiumi|WD=Q3545159|lt=Kami-umi}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=rainmaking rites|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|en|Ta-no-Kami|WD=Q7683716|lt=rice field deities}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|Child|en|Child|WD=Q7569|lt=children}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with {{ill|Pregnancy|en|Pregnancy|WD=Q11995|lt=Pregnancy|1=Pregnancy}} and {{ill|Childbirth|en|Childbirth|WD=Q34581|lt=Childbirth|1=Childbirth}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means {{ill|Water|en|Water|WD=Q283|lt=Water|1=Water}} {{ill|Distribution|en|Distribution|WD=Q225802|lt=Distribution|1=Distribution}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|Suijin|WD=Q3137449|lt=Suijin|1=Suijin}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In {{ill|Japanese mythology|en|Japanese mythology|WD=Q814158|lt=Japanese mythology|1=Japanese mythology}}, during the {{ill|Kamiumi|en|Kamiumi|WD=Q3545159|lt=Kami-umi|1=Kamiumi}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=Rainmaking (ritual)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|en|Ta-no-Kami|WD=Q7683716|lt=rice field deities|1=Ta-no-Kami}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|Child|en|Child|WD=Q7569|lt=children|1=Child}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with {{ill|Pregnancy|en|Pregnancy|WD=Q11995|lt=Pregnancy|1=Pregnancy}} and {{ill|Childbirth|en|Childbirth|WD=Q34581|lt=Childbirth|1=Childbirth}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means {{ill|Water|en|Water|WD=Q283|lt=Water|1=Water}} {{ill|Distribution|en|Distribution|WD=Q225802|lt=Distribution|1=Distribution}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|Suijin|WD=Q3137449|lt=Suijin|1=Suijin}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In {{ill|Japanese mythology|en|Japanese mythology|WD=Q814158|lt=Japanese mythology|1=Japanese mythology}}, during the {{ill|Kamiumi|en|Kamiumi|WD=Q3545159|lt=Kami-umi|1=Kamiumi}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=Rainmaking (ritual)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|en|Ta-no-Kami|WD=Q7683716|lt=rice field deities|1=Ta-no-Kami}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|Child|en|Child|WD=Q7569|lt=children|1=Child}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with {{ill|Pregnancy|en|Pregnancy|WD=Q11995|lt=Pregnancy|1=Pregnancy}} and {{ill|Childbirth|en|Childbirth|WD=Q34581|lt=Childbirth|1=Childbirth}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means {{ill|Water|en|Water|WD=Q283|lt=Water|1=Water}} {{ill|Distribution|en|Distribution|WD=Q225802|lt=Distribution|1=Distribution}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|Suijin|WD=Q3137449|lt=Suijin|1=Suijin}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" /> 

==Overview==

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In {{ill|Japanese mythology|en|Japanese mythology|WD=Q814158|lt=Japanese mythology|1=Japanese mythology}}, during the {{ill|Kamiumi|en|Kamiumi|WD=Q3545159|lt=Kami-umi|1=Kamiumi}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=Rainmaking (ritual)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|en|Ta-no-Kami|WD=Q7683716|lt=rice field deities|1=Ta-no-Kami}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|Child|en|Child|WD=Q7569|lt=children|1=Child}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.

'''Mikumari-no-kami''' (水分神) is a Japanese [[kami]] where she is worshipped at {{ill|Uda Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uda Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎and {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|qq=}} ‎<ref name="web.archive.org-2023">{{Cite web|date=2023-06-02|title=Mikumarinokami {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230602115915/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9711|access-date=2024-05-24|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>. Due to a pun she is associated with {{ill|Pregnancy|en|Pregnancy|WD=Q11995|lt=Pregnancy|1=Pregnancy}} and {{ill|Childbirth|en|Childbirth|WD=Q34581|lt=Childbirth|1=Childbirth}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-03 |title=Yoshino Mikumari Shrine - Nara |url=https://en.japantravel.com/nara/yoshino-mikumari-shrine/22951 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=JapanTravel |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Mikumari Shrine {{!}} Things to Do in Yoshino {{!}} All Japan Tours|url=https://alljapantours.com/japan-attraction/shrines/kansai/mikumari-shrine/|access-date=2024-03-25|website=alljapantours.com}}</ref>

The most famous '''mikumari''' shrine is that of Yoshino<ref name="Grapard-1982">{{Cite journal |last=Grapard |first=Allan G. |date=1982 |title=Flying Mountains and Walkers of Emptiness: Toward a Definition of Sacred Space in Japanese Religions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062158 |journal=History of Religions |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=195–221 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>. Such shrines are frequently found in mountains and linked to Buddhism through {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|4=fr|5=Shinbutsu shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> The etymology means {{ill|Water|en|Water|WD=Q283|lt=Water|1=Water}} {{ill|Distribution|en|Distribution|WD=Q225802|lt=Distribution|1=Distribution}}.<ref name="Grapard-1982" /> As tutelary deity of water management, Mikumari is specially honored, frequently linked to the origins of agricultural irrigation systems. She is seen as a guardian watching over fertility and facilitating childbirth, as opposed to {{ill|Suijin|en|Suijin|WD=Q3137449|lt=Suijin|1=Suijin}} who is more about water in general, including water safety and sewage management.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com">{{Cite web|title=Suijin, Water Divinity of Japan, Shinto Origin, Patron of Fishermen, Fertility, Motherhood|url=https://www.onmarkproductions.com/html/suijin.html|access-date=2024-04-02|website=www.onmarkproductions.com}}</ref>

In Japanese mythology, it is said that Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Heavenly Water Distribution) and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami (God of Earthly Water Distribution) were the children of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ|en:draft|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|8=fr|9=User:Immanuelle/Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|qq=}} .<ref name="web.archive.org-2023" />

Suijin, in Japanese Shintoism, refers to the numerous celestial and terrestrial manifestations of the benevolent water deity, encompassing a wide range of mythological creatures related to water. Mikumari, as the "kami of water distribution", is revered in this specific context, often associated with the sources of agricultural waterways and considered protective in the areas of fertility and easy childbirth. While Suijin is honored at a multitude of shrines across Japan for its protection over fishermen and its patronage of fertility, Mikumari is specifically invoked for the distribution and management of water, a vital aspect for agriculture.<ref name="www.onmarkproductions.com" />

The name "Kumari" derives from the term "kubari" (配り), meaning "distribution," and these deities are often enshrined at water sources and distribution points such as springs and river junctions.

In {{ill|Japanese mythology|en|Japanese mythology|WD=Q814158|lt=Japanese mythology|1=Japanese mythology}}, during the {{ill|Kamiumi|en|Kamiumi|WD=Q3545159|lt=Kami-umi|1=Kamiumi}} (birth of gods) segment, the deities '''Ame no Mikumari no Kami''' (天水分神) and '''Kuni no Mikumari no Kami''' (国水分神) are described as the offspring of {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhiko|ja|ハヤアキツヒコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}} and {{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|lt=Hayaakitsuhime|ja|ハヤアキツヒメ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ}}.

As water-related deities, they are often worshipped for {{ill|rainmaking|ja|祈雨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rainmaking|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 雨乞い|1=Rainmaking (ritual)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q477738}} and associated with {{ill|Ta-no-Kami|en|Ta-no-Kami|WD=Q7683716|lt=rice field deities|1=Ta-no-Kami}} or, when enshrined at water sources, with {{ill|mountain deities|ja|山の神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mountain deities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Yama-no-Kami|WD=Q839254}}. Later, the term "Mikumari" was interpreted as "Mikomori" (御子守), leading to their veneration as guardians of {{ill|Child|en|Child|WD=Q7569|lt=children|1=Child}} and as deities of childbearing and safe childbirth.
